steps.instruction: The \(F\)-statistic is a ratio of between-group to within-group variation. **Predict first.**

gate.question: If all the group means are truly equal (\(H_0\)), what should \(F\) be near?

choices.text: Near 1 — between-group and within-group variation are similar

gate.feedback: Right. Under \(H_0\) the numerator (spread of group means) and denominator (scatter within groups) both estimate the same error variance, so \(F \approx 1\). A large \(F\) is the signal of a real difference.
gate.retryFeedback: Both parts of \(F\) estimate the same variance when \(H_0\) holds — so their ratio sits near 1, not 0.

steps.instruction: Pick any multi-group numeric dataset (3+ groups of a quantitative response). State H₀ and Hₐ in your head.
steps.observe: What does Hₐ actually claim - that ALL group means differ, or that AT LEAST ONE differs?
steps.reveal: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = ... = μₖ vs. Hₐ: AT LEAST ONE μᵢ differs from the others. The F-test never tells you all are different - and never tells you which one is different.

steps.instruction: Look at the side-by-side boxplots the tool displays. Eyeball whether within-group spreads look roughly equal and whether each group is roughly symmetric.
steps.observe: Does the largest group SD look more than ~2x the smallest? Any group with extreme skew or outliers?
steps.reveal: If spreads are wildly different or a group has a strong outlier, ANOVA's assumptions are stretched. Switch to /simulate/randomization-anova/ in that situation - it makes no normality or equal-variance assumption.

steps.instruction: Run the F-test. Note F, the two df values (between = k - 1, within = N - k), and the p-value.
steps.observe: What is your decision at α = 0.05?
steps.reveal: At α = 0.05 reject H₀ iff p < 0.05. F = (between-group variance) / (within-group variance). Under H₀ both estimate the same noise and F is approximately 1. Large F means between-group differences are bigger than within-group noise can explain by chance.

steps.instruction: Suppose H₀ is rejected. A student writes 'all three groups have different means.' Why is that wrong?
steps.observe: What follow-up would tell you WHICH pairs of groups actually differ?
steps.reveal: Hₐ says AT LEAST ONE differs, not all. To identify which pairs, run a POST-HOC procedure (Tukey HSD, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons) - those control the family-wise Type I error rate across multiple pairwise tests. A bare F-rejection is the green light to ask WHICH; it is not the answer.

steps.instruction: Open /simulate/randomization-anova/ on the same data (new tab) and run 5000 shuffles. Compare its p-value to the F-distribution's.
steps.observe: How close are the two p-values?
steps.reveal: On well-behaved data the two p-values agree closely - the F distribution is a good approximation. On data with small groups, outliers, or unequal variances they diverge; the simulation is the safer report. The F-test is a convenient shortcut; the randomization is the gold standard.

steps.instruction: Before you finish, put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: What do the numerator and denominator of \(F\) measure, and why does \(F\) near 1 support \(H_0\)?
A significant \(F\) lets you conclude 'at least one mean differs.' Why can't you conclude that all groups differ from each other?

respond.answer: A strong answer: \(F = \text{MSG}/\text{MSE}\) compares between-group variation (how far the group means spread from the grand mean) to within-group variation (scatter inside groups). Under \(H_0\) both estimate the same error variance, so \(F\approx 1\); a large \(F\) means the means spread more than chance alone would produce. Rejecting \(H_0\) says **at least one** mean differs — the omnibus test doesn't say which or how many; that needs a post-hoc comparison.
